name: Agriculture
blurb: Vision-guided spraying, yield prediction, and autonomous equipment at commercial scale, tracked through USDA ERS, FAO, satellite data providers, and the equipment and standards bodies.

points.desc: Deere's precision agriculture line (See and Spray, autonomous tractors) is the reference commercial deployment.
points.name: Precision ag is shipping product

points.desc: Census BTOS covers agriculture-adjacent sectors in its fortnightly AI-use series.
points.name: Adoption is measured, not guessed

points.desc: The Economic Research Service publishes the data series on precision-agriculture adoption across US farms - variable-rate technology, yield monitoring, autonomous equipment. The federal measurement layer.
points.name: USDA ERS measures US adoption

points.desc: The UN Food and Agriculture Organization's digital agriculture program, with the 60 Decibels-supported Digital Agriculture Index, benchmarks platform adoption and real-world yield and income impact.
points.name: FAO benchmarks digital agriculture globally

points.desc: The AgriFoodTech investment research tracks venture capital into agricultural AI, robotics, computer vision, and farm-management software - the sector's funding barometer.
points.name: AgFunder indexes the investment flow

points.desc: Planet Labs' high-resolution imagery, Descartes Labs' geospatial ML, and EarthDaily's field-level crop indicators supply the AI-ready observation data behind yield prediction and crop-stress detection.
points.name: The satellite layer feeds the models

points.desc: The Association of Equipment Manufacturers covers autonomous machinery, AI hardware standards, and robotics adoption across crop and livestock production.
points.name: AEM tracks the machinery standards

points.desc: The nonprofit consortium sets the open data standards that let AI models ingest feeds from tractors, drones, soil sensors, and satellites - the plumbing under everything else.
points.name: AgGateway makes the data interoperable

points.desc: The International Society of Precision Agriculture is the scientific organization connecting academic research on remote sensing and spatial analytics to commercial practice.
points.name: ISPA bridges the science and the field

points.desc: The 100 Million Farmers initiative tracks AI adoption through the lens of climate-smart and regenerative agriculture metrics globally.
points.name: WEF tracks climate-smart adoption

points.desc: Bayer's Climate FieldView and Corteva's Granular are the large digital-farming platforms turning soil, weather, and yield data into planting and input prescriptions with machine learning.
points.name: The agribusiness platforms run the prescriptions

points.desc: CNH Industrial's Raven division builds driverless tractor technology, AI path-planning, and precision application - the equipment layer beyond Deere.
points.name: CNH and Raven automate the other fleets

points.desc: Carbon Robotics' LaserWeeder kills weeds with computer vision and lasers instead of herbicide; Monarch builds electric driverless tractors - narrow AI shipping as farm equipment.
points.name: The pure-plays attack single problems

summary: Precision agriculture - vision-guided spraying, yield prediction, autonomous equipment - is deployed at commercial scale. Who tracks it: federal adoption data, a UN benchmarking framework, a venture index, and standards bodies, layered over the equipment giants and AI pure-plays actually shipping it.

analysis.body:
# Agriculture AI Deployment and Investment

AI adoption in agriculture remains measured but concentrated in specific, high-value applications. The Census Bureau has been tracking AI use in agriculture since September 2023, with prior-period data showing 13.7% of farms reporting AI use in the two weeks preceding the survey, though the most recent figure is suppressed. This adoption reflects deployment across a narrower range of use cases than the sector's size might suggest. AgFunder indexes the investment flow and reported that global agrifoodtech funding reached $16.2 billion in 2025, nearly flat year-on-year at a minus 3% change from 2024, signaling that investor capital, while substantial, is consolidating around companies with "tangible science, real unit economics, and clear paths to revenue" rather than spreading broadly across the industry.

The deployed applications cluster in precision agriculture, autonomous equipment, and data-driven input management. Climate FieldView, the Bayer platform profiled in the excerpts, shows concrete ROI: farmers using FieldView seed scripts saw an average increase of +5 bu/ac compared to users who wrote their own scripts, a direct yield lift that vendors cite as proof of concept. Carbon Robotics operates in weed management with its LaserWeeder system, which uses computer vision and autonomous lasers to eliminate weeds, reducing herbicide dependency while lowering farm input costs. These implementations rely on a data plumbing layer that AgGateway, the nonprofit interoperability consortium, has built through open data standards that allow AI models to ingest feeds from tractors, drones, soil sensors, and satellites. The satellite data itself comes from providers like Planet Labs, which supplies high-resolution daily Earth imagery that feeds crop monitoring and yield prediction models.

Equipment manufacturers have become a primary locus of AI embedding. The Association of Equipment Manufacturers (AEM) coordinates autonomous machinery standards and hardware integration, while Deere's precision agriculture line (See and Spray vision-guided spraying and autonomous tractors) remains the reference commercial deployment in the sector. CNH Industrial's Raven division builds driverless tractor technology and AI path-planning beyond Deere's offerings. This concentration of capability in large OEMs and platform providers suggests that AI in agriculture is not a commodity adoption pattern but rather a function of capital and technical depth in equipment design and software integration, limiting how widely these tools can diffuse.

Investment patterns show regional divergence. AgFunder reported that agrifoodtech funding in Asia-Pacific (APAC) reached $4.2 billion by end of October 2024, a 38% increase from the $3.1 billion raised over the same period in 2023, indicating recovery in developed markets like the US and Netherlands alongside growth in India. African agrifoodtech funding showed only mild growth, raising $145 million in the first half of 2024, a 1.6% year-over-year increase but representing just 1.6% of global investment. This geographic clustering around North America, Western Europe, and India reflects both the cost of AI-ready infrastructure (satellites, wireless connectivity, equipment interoperability standards) and the concentration of farm sizes and market structures capable of absorbing precision-agriculture premium pricing.

The scientific and standards infrastructure supporting agricultural AI is distributed across multiple organizations but integrated in purpose. The International Society of Precision Agriculture (ISPA) bridges academic research on remote sensing and spatial analytics to commercial practice through its scientific membership and annual conferences. The FAO's digital agriculture program benchmarks platform adoption and real-world yield and income impact globally, providing the measurement layer outside the US that USDA ERS supplies domestically. Neither source reports specific AI adoption percentages for their covered regions, but their existence indicates that measurement frameworks are in place and maturing. For farms considering AI deployment, the clearest takeaway is that ROI appears tied to specific, narrow applications (seed prescription, weed detection, input optimization) rather than blanket AI adoption, and that success requires equipment capable of data capture, integration into an established platform like FieldView or Granular, and sufficient scale to justify integration costs.
